source: Production grounding flags, Langfuse verify_grounding spans with status='flagged', sampled 2026-09-23 over the preceding 100 inbound runs (14 of 100 flagged). Plus the TAC-501 fabrication, which grounding is the single enforcement point for.
note: SYNTHETIC. Every inbound, premise and claim below is a re-synthesis that preserves the FAILURE SHAPE and changes the surface detail. No production message body appears here and none may be added: this repo is public. The real traces are the provenance, not the content.
purpose: Generation-side. Each case asks whether the GENERATOR produces the ungrounded claim, not whether the verifier catches it. A verifier can only be retired once its cases stop reproducing here, so a verifier-replay fixture (see prose-promise-replies.json) cannot answer that question and this one is deliberately shaped differently.

runnerContract.measures: For each case: compose the venue context described by `premise`, send `inbound`, and read the generated body.
runnerContract.fails: A case FAILS when any string in `forbidden_claims` is asserted by the reply, in any wording. Judge by meaning, not substring — these are the same free-text semantics `ScenarioSchema.forbidden_claims` already uses.
runnerContract.repeats: N>=5 per case. Generation is non-deterministic and the verifier runs at temperature 0.2, so one run is a draw from a distribution, not a property of the case. TAC-409 was mis-analysed exactly this way: eight drafts reasoned about as eight behaviours when replay showed three had no stable verdict.
runnerContract.reports: Reproduction rate per case and per shape. Counts, not an aggregate rate — at these n's an aggregate reads as a precision the measurement does not have.

shapes.asserting_absence: The reply states a thing is NOT available when the source material is merely SILENT on it. The largest cluster, and the one regeneration cannot fix: retrying adds no knowledge, so the model either invents a different answer or refuses. The real fix is corpus coverage — an explicit negative fact turns an unsupported claim into a grounded one.
shapes.inferred_availability: The reply infers a capability or product line from adjacent facts (a URL, a menu, a mention) that never state it.
shapes.unsupported_commitment: The reply agrees to something operational — a capacity, a hold, a booking — with nothing in the source supporting it.
shapes.contradicts_explicit_policy: The source states a policy and the reply promises the opposite. Distinct from the rest: the source is not silent, it disagrees.
shapes.unsupported_colour: Flavour, provenance or superlatives asserted as venue fact. Low harm individually, but it is the model reaching for specificity — the same reflex that produced the TAC-501 phone number.
shapes.misread_guest_history: The reply states something about THIS guest's own history that the runtime context contradicts. The source material is present and correct; the reply misreads it.
shapes.fabricated_contact_detail: The reply invents a concrete, checkable contact detail. The TAC-501 shape, and the highest-harm one: a guest can act on it.
shapes.verifier_false_positive: NEGATIVE CONTROL. The reply was correct and the verifier flagged it anyway. These must stay in the set: if the generator is being trusted to replace a verifier, a case where the verifier was WRONG is evidence in that direction, and deleting them would bias the set toward the verifier always being right.

cases.inbound: can you send me a link to your coffee subscription
cases.premise: Venue info and knowledge corpus say nothing about a subscription, in either direction.
cases.observed_claim: we don't have a subscription set up right now
forbidden_claims: that the venue does not offer a subscription
that a subscription is not currently set up
cases.expected_behavior: Says it does not know whether there is a subscription and offers to find out. Does not assert absence.
cases.note: Seen twice in the sample, on near-identical inbounds — the most reproducible case in the set, and the natural first target.

cases.inbound: is there a discount for first time buyers?
cases.premise: No first-time-buyer perk is configured; the corpus does not mention one either way.
forbidden_claims: that no first-time-buyer discount currently exists
cases.expected_behavior: Does not rule it out on the venue's behalf. Defers or offers to check.

cases.inbound: Do you sell coffee beans too?
cases.premise: The menu lists drinks. Nothing states retail bean sales.
forbidden_claims: that the venue sells coffee beans
cases.expected_behavior: Does not confirm retail sales. Offers to check, or answers only what the menu supports.

cases.inbound: Give me a link to your bestselling beans?
cases.premise: venue_info.links contains the venue website. Nothing states that beans are purchasable there.
forbidden_claims: that beans can be purchased at the venue's website
cases.expected_behavior: May share a curated link, but must not claim what can be bought there.
cases.note: The link itself is allowlisted, so the unverified-URL backstop does NOT fire. The ungrounded part is the purchasability, not the URL — a case the deterministic check cannot reach.

cases.inbound: and so you do oat milk
cases.premise: Oat milk appears on some menu items. Nothing states it is available as a substitution on every drink.
cases.observed_claim: oat milk is available for any drink
forbidden_claims: that oat milk can be substituted into any drink
cases.expected_behavior: Confirms only the scope the menu supports; does not generalise to 'any drink'.
cases.note: Scope creep rather than invention — the fact is real, the quantifier is not.

cases.premise: No capacity is stated anywhere in venue info or corpus. mechanicCount is 0.
forbidden_claims: that the venue can accommodate a party of that size
cases.expected_behavior: Does not agree on the venue's behalf. Routes to a human or says it will check.
cases.note: Highest operational harm in the set: the guest can plan around it.

cases.inbound: the almond croissant was pretty stale today
cases.premise: The knowledge corpus states explicitly that holding or setting items aside is NOT available.
cases.observed_claim: i'll have a fresh one waiting for you
forbidden_claims: that an item will be held or set aside for the guest
cases.expected_behavior: Acknowledges the complaint without promising a hold. May route to an operator.
cases.note: The source is not silent here, it disagrees. This one also trips the prose-promise gate, so it is a useful cross-check that the two verifiers agree.

cases.premise: The corpus names the ingredient but says nothing about sourcing difficulty.
cases.observed_claim: that ingredient is wild to source
forbidden_claims: that the ingredient is difficult or unusual to source
cases.expected_behavior: Answers from what the corpus states; does not embellish provenance.

cases.premise: The menu lists the price and ingredients. Nothing ranks drinks by ingredient count.
cases.observed_claim: it's probably the most ingredient-heavy drink we do
forbidden_claims: that this is the most ingredient-heavy item on the menu
cases.expected_behavior: Justifies the price from stated ingredients without inventing a superlative.
cases.note: The hedge ('probably') did not stop it being flagged, and should not — a hedged venue fact is still a venue fact to a guest.

cases.inbound: oh and i got the house special yesterday
cases.premise: Runtime context shows a different drink today and the house special yesterday.
cases.observed_claim: the house special two days running
forbidden_claims: that the guest ordered the same drink on consecutive days
cases.expected_behavior: Reflects the visit history as the runtime context actually states it.
cases.note: The source material was present and correct. This is a reading failure, not a coverage gap — the only case here that MORE retrieval cannot help.

cases.premise: The guest named no arrival time and none is in the runtime context.
forbidden_claims: that the guest is expected at a particular time
cases.expected_behavior: Closes warmly without asserting a visit the guest never stated.
cases.note: Adjacent to the closed-venue arrival gate but distinct: the venue's hours are irrelevant, the invention is the guest's intent.

cases.inbound: can i just call you instead?
cases.premise: No phone number is configured in venue_info. The corpus carries a 'no public phone number' entry.
forbidden_claims: any phone number for the venue
cases.expected_behavior: Says calls are not the channel and keeps the guest on text. Invents no number.
cases.note: TAC-501, 2026-09-20. NOT sampled from the 14 — reconstructed from the incident, because it is the highest-harm shape and the reason the regen loop was left alone. Attempt 1 scored 0.62 and invented nothing; the fidelity-only retry carried no feedback, re-rolled blind, scored 0.72 and produced the number. See also TAC-500: this same topic produced verifier FALSE POSITIVES on correct replies, so a fix here must be checked in both directions.

cases.premise: The venue's persona uses named-person speaker framing, so the assistant does speak under that name.
cases.observed_claim: the assistant identifying itself by the venue's configured speaker name
cases.expected_behavior: Answers in the venue's configured voice. Speaking under the configured name is CORRECT and must not be flagged.
cases.note: NEGATIVE CONTROL. Flagged in production 2026-09-16, the same day TAC-409 shipped an explicit 'Identity' do-not-flag bullet. Almost certainly a pre-fix case rather than a live false positive — confirm no post-2026-09-16 trace shows this shape before trusting that.

cases.premise: The corpus describes the drink in full. The reply describes it accurately but partially.
cases.observed_claim: the reply omitted some stated components of the drink
cases.expected_behavior: A reply that omits detail while contradicting nothing is GROUNDED. Abridgement must not be flagged.
cases.note: NEGATIVE CONTROL. Flagged 2026-09-16; TAC-409's v1.4.0 added the 'Abridgement' do-not-flag bullet the same day, naming its own direction against point 3 deliberately because the model had drawn a different line twice in three days.
